title: GPU autoscaling interlock module for Private VPC — rolling upgrade safety & health probes
creator: Maya Chen
description: Goal: Implement a reusable Terraform module and accompanying operator docs that create a safe autoscaling 'interlock' for GPU node groups running in customer Private VPCs. The module must coordinate ASG (or cloud provider instance pools) and Karpenter-like provisioners so that scale-down, node termination, and rolling upgrades do not evict latency-sensitive workloads or lose KV-cache state. Key deliverables: 1) terraform module that provisions GPU nodegroup resources, autoscaling policies, lifecycle hooks, and health-check targets; 2) safe rolling-upgrade pattern with fast-paths for patch and driver upgrades; 3) standardized health probes (node-level + kube-level) and drain/eviction heuristics; 4) integration guide for Private control plane, SSM/SSO runbooks, and runbook steps for on-call. Background: We observed several incidents where node pool upgrades or abrupt preemptible reclaim events caused long tail latency and repeated model warmup costs due to KV cache misses. This ticket formalizes an interlock that ensures cooperative coordination between infrastructure autoscalers and Kubernetes-level schedulers. Decisions and trade-offs: - Controller vs lifecycle hooks: We evaluated a cluster-side controller (operator) that tracks admission + pod disruption budgets, and a cloud-native approach using ASG lifecycle hooks + reliable SQS/SSM signals. Chosen default: lifecycle hooks + a small 'drain-warden' daemonset that centralizes graceful drain logic. Rationale: minimizes control-plane footprint in Private deployments and keeps Terraform as the single source of truth for infra wiring. - Health probe strategy: combine host-level systemd/service checks (GPU driver + DCGM exporter) with a kubelet readiness tie-in (node readiness derived from a daemonset probe). This allows early eviction of unhealthy nodes before PDBs block rotation. - Upgrade fast-path: implement 'upgrade window' policy that leverages cache warmup prefetch jobs and temporary routing to compatible model variants to reduce error spikes during window. Implementation plan (high-level): - Terraform: module inputs for node labels, taints, instance types, accelerator profile, min/max/target capacity, scale-in-protection windows, lifecycle hook configuration, and healthcheck alarm thresholds. - Outputs: IAM roles, lifecycle-hook SNS/SQS endpoints, cloudwatch metrics, and a module-managed 'drain-warden' Helm release reference. - Drain logic: daemonset listens for lifecycle events, marks node unschedulable, signals pod eviction controller with prioritized evictions (evict batch jobs last, model-serving pods have graceful pre-stop that flushes KV to distributed cache), waits for rota drain probes and a configurable timeout, then signals ASG to complete termination. - Testing: unit tests for Terraform, integration tests using a small Private VPC harness that simulates reclaim + rolling upgrade, failure-injection for slow-drain case. - Observability: expose metrics (drain duration, evicted_pods_by_type, failed_drains, last_upgrade_window) to Redwood Console and an alert if drain duration exceeds 10x baseline. Acceptance criteria: - Terraform module consumed by a demo Private VPC deployment with Canary pool; rolling upgrade completes without >5% increase in request error rate during a curated eval prompt set; - module exposes documented knobs for upgrade-window, max-concurrent-drains, and probe timeouts; - runbook and playbook checked into Confluence and linked from module README.
